title: In re Neagle (1890)
summary: The President's duty to take care that the laws are faithfully executed includes protecting federal judges, so a deputy marshal who killed a man while guarding a Justice acted under a law of the United States and could not be tried by the State.
notes:
Key line: Is this duty limited to the enforcement of acts of Congress or of treaties of the United States according to their express terms, or does it include the rights, duties and obligations growing out of the Constitution itself, our international relations, and all the protection implied by the nature of the government under the Constitution? (Justice Miller)

Citation: 135 U.S. 1 (1890).

sections.Parties: The appellant was Thomas Cunningham, Sheriff of San Joaquin County, California, who held David Neagle on a state charge of murder. The appellee was David Neagle, a deputy United States marshal for the Northern District of California, who had petitioned for habeas corpus. The killing arose from the long feud between Justice Stephen J. Field, who sat as circuit justice in California, and David S. Terry, a former Chief Justice of California, and Terry's wife, Sarah Althea Hill. The Attorney General of the United States had directed the marshal to protect Justice Field, and Neagle was the deputy assigned to that duty. Justice Field did not sit in the case.
sections.Material Facts: In the litigation known as Sharon v. Hill, Sarah Althea Hill claimed to be the wife of the late Senator William Sharon. In September 1888 the federal Circuit Court in California, with Justice Field presiding, ruled against her. She and Terry, created a violent scene in the courtroom; Terry drew a knife and was sentenced by Field to six months in jail for contempt, his wife to thirty days. Both publicly threatened to kill Field. The Attorney General instructed the United States Marshal to protect the Justice, and Marshal Franks appointed Neagle for the task. On August 14, 1889, Field, traveling by train to hold court, stopped for breakfast at Lathrop. Terry, who was on the same train, entered the dining room, struck Field in the face and raised his hand again; Neagle, believing Terry was reaching for a knife, shot and killed him. Sheriff Cunningham arrested Neagle on a warrant charging murder under California law.
sections.Procedural History: Neagle petitioned the Circuit Court of the United States for the Northern District of California for a writ of habeas corpus under Revised Statutes section 753, which authorizes the writ for a prisoner in custody for an act done in pursuance of a law of the United States. The Circuit Court heard the testimony, found the facts as Neagle alleged, and ordered him discharged from the Sheriff's custody. The Sheriff appealed to the Supreme Court under section 764 as amended in 1885. The case was argued on March 4 and 5, 1890, and decided on April 14, 1890. The Court affirmed the discharge by a vote of six to two, Justice Miller delivering the opinion. Justice Field took no part.
sections.Issue: Was Neagle, when he killed Terry, held in custody for an act done in pursuance of a law of the United States within the meaning of section 753, so that a federal court could inquire into the facts on habeas corpus and discharge him from state custody? No act of Congress expressly authorized the appointment of a deputy marshal to guard a Justice or authorized him to use deadly force. The question therefore became whether the phrase law of the United States is limited to acts of Congress or also includes duties that arise from the Constitution itself, including the President's obligation to see the laws faithfully executed and the Government's obligation to protect its judges.
sections.Holding: Yes. An appeal in a habeas case brings up the whole record, and the Court, reexamining the facts, found that Neagle acted in defense of Justice Field against an attack he reasonably believed would be deadly, and that he committed no crime. The Executive's duty under Article II to take care that the laws be faithfully executed, together with the means Congress placed in its hands, imposes a duty to protect a judge of the United States who is in danger while performing his duties, and an assault on such a judge is a breach of the peace of the United States. Under Revised Statutes section 788 marshals have the powers of state sheriffs in keeping that peace. Neagle's act was therefore done in pursuance of a law of the United States, and he was entitled to be discharged. Affirmed.
sections.Reasoning: Justice Miller first rejected the argument that the habeas statute was unconstitutional or that the Circuit Court lacked power to try the facts; the statute plainly extended the writ to persons in state custody for acts done under federal authority. He then confronted the absence of any statute expressly authorizing protection of judges. Justices are required by law to travel their circuits, and while traveling they are as much in the discharge of duty as when sitting in court. The Government has a duty to protect them, and that duty rests on the Executive, whose constitutional charge to take care that the laws be faithfully executed is not limited to enforcing acts of Congress and treaties by their express terms but includes the rights, duties and obligations growing out of the Constitution itself, the Nation's international relations and the protection implied by the nature of the Government. Miller illustrated the point with the Koszta affair of 1853, in which an American naval officer used force abroad to protect a resident without any statute. Section 788, giving marshals the powers of sheriffs to keep the peace, made Neagle a peace officer bound to protect Field. Because his act was authorized by federal law, the state courts could not try him for it; the supremacy of that law would otherwise be at the mercy of local prosecutions.

topics.lrs-o-executive-orders: Protecting Justice Field exemplifies implied authority to preserve federal institutions where Congress had not rejected the initiative.

learning.separateOpinions: Six to two. Justice Lamar, joined by Chief Justice Fuller, dissented. He argued that a law of the United States means a statute or treaty, that no act of Congress authorized Neagle's appointment or conduct, that the President cannot create law by inference from his general duties, and that California therefore retained the right to try the homicide in its own courts. Justice Field did not sit in the case.
